 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

schema.name: SendUserFile
schema.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. // Seed data: a believable, fully-populated "battery" workflow for the BMW 5
// Series so every view (landing, PM workflow, stakeholder review, audit
// trail) has something real to render on first load. Other components are
// left empty so the landing page's "create new workflow" path is also
// demonstrable.
//
// Swap-out point for Role A: once real datasets (verbatims, equipment,
// sales, study) are uploaded, replace buildSeed()'s battery fixtures with
// an ingest() pipeline that produces the same shapes.

import { nanoid } from "nanoid";
import type {
  Vehicle,
  VehicleComponent,
  Workflow,
  Requirement,
  Signal,
  SourceRecord,
  Stakeholder,
  StakeholderReview,
  AuditLogEntry,
  AISummary,
} from "./types";

const VEHICLE_ID = "veh_5series";
const COMPONENT_BATTERY_ID = "comp_battery";
const WORKFLOW_ID = "wf_battery_demo";

export function buildSeed() {
  const vehicles: Vehicle[] = [
    {
      id: VEHICLE_ID,
      name: "BMW 5 Series",
      generation: "Next generation (successor to G60)",
      markets: ["Europe", "China", "United States"],
    },
  ];

  const components: VehicleComponent[] = [
    { id: COMPONENT_BATTERY_ID, vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID, key: "battery", label: "Battery & Charging", hotspot: { xPct: 49, yPct: 61 }, workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID },
    { id: "comp_exterior", vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID, key: "exterior", label: "Exterior & Design", hotspot: { xPct: 50, yPct: 76 }, workflowId: null },
    { id: "comp_interior", vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID, key: "interior", label: "Interior & Cabin", hotspot: { xPct: 61, yPct: 46 }, workflowId: null },
    { id: "comp_windows", vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID, key: "windows", label: "Windows & Glass", hotspot: { xPct: 76, yPct: 38 }, workflowId: null },
    { id: "comp_steering", vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID, key: "steering", label: "Steering & Cockpit", hotspot: { xPct: 58, yPct: 50 }, workflowId: null },
    { id: "comp_engine", vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID, key: "engine", label: "Powertrain", hotspot: { xPct: 24, yPct: 59 }, workflowId: null },
  ];

  const now = new Date();
  const daysAgo = (n: number) => new Date(now.getTime() - n * 86400000).toISOString();

  const workflow: Workflow = {
    id: WORKFLOW_ID,
    vehicleId: VEHICLE_ID,
    componentId: COMPONENT_BATTERY_ID,
    market: "Europe",
    status: "pm_review",
    stages: [
      { key: "ingest", label: "Ingest datasets", status: "complete", startedAt: daysAgo(9), completedAt: daysAgo(9), owner: "pm" },
      { key: "enrich", label: "Enrich with web knowledge", status: "complete", startedAt: daysAgo(9), completedAt: daysAgo(8), owner: "ai" },
      { key: "extract", label: "Extract signals", status: "complete", startedAt: daysAgo(8), completedAt: daysAgo(8), owner: "ai" },
      { key: "derive", label: "Derive requirements", status: "complete", startedAt: daysAgo(8), completedAt: daysAgo(7), owner: "ai" },
      { key: "score", label: "Score & prioritize", status: "complete", startedAt: daysAgo(7), completedAt: daysAgo(7), owner: "ai" },
      { key: "stakeholder_review", label: "Stakeholder review", status: "complete", startedAt: daysAgo(6), completedAt: daysAgo(2), owner: "stakeholder" },
      { key: "pm_decision", label: "PM decision", status: "active", startedAt: daysAgo(2), completedAt: null, owner: "pm" },
      { key: "deploy", label: "Move to deploy", status: "pending", startedAt: null, completedAt: null, owner: "pm" },
    ],
    createdAt: daysAgo(9),
    updatedAt: daysAgo(0),
  };

  // ---------- sources ----------
  const sources: SourceRecord[] = [
    { id: "src_verb_1", workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID, datasetType: "verbatim", reliability: "first_party", title: "Verbatim #4471 (EU, i5 owner)", excerpt: "\"DC fast charging from 10-80% takes nearly 30 minutes at the stations near me, Hyundai does it in 18.\"", url: null, retrievedAt: daysAgo(9) },
    { id: "src_verb_2", workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID, datasetType: "verbatim", reliability: "first_party", title: "Verbatim #4502 (EU, i5 owner)", excerpt: "\"The range the car shows me in winter is way off from what I actually get. I never trust it.\"", url: null, retrievedAt: daysAgo(9) },
    { id: "src_verb_3", workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID, datasetType: "verbatim", reliability: "first_party", title: "Verbatim #4588 (EU, i5 owner)", excerpt: "\"Love that I can precondition the battery from the app before a trip, keep that.\"", url: null, retrievedAt: daysAgo(9) },
    { id: "src_study_1", workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID, datasetType: "study", reliability: "first_party", title: "Customer study: charging satisfaction (EU, n=612)", excerpt: "Charging speed satisfaction: 58/100 (category average 71/100). Range accuracy trust: 49/100.", url: null, retrievedAt: daysAgo(9) },
    { id: "src_equip_1", workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID, datasetType: "equipment", reliability: "first_party", title: "Equipment list: current 5 Series eDrive", excerpt: "Max DC charging: 205 kW, 10-80% in ~28 min (WLTP). No standard battery health readout.", url: null, retrievedAt: daysAgo(9) },
    { id: "src_sales_1", workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID, datasetType: "sales", reliability: "first_party", title: "Sales volumes by powertrain, EU, last 4 quarters", excerpt: "BEV mix of 5 Series sales grew from 19% to 31% QoQ in EU; China BEV mix at 44%.", url: null, retrievedAt: daysAgo(9) },

  // ---- local helpers ----
  function weightedScore(req: Requirement): number {
    const totalWeight = req.scoreFactors.reduce((s, f) => s + f.weight, 0) || 1;
    const weighted = req.scoreFactors.reduce((s, f) => s + f.rawValue * f.weight, 0);
    return Math.round((weighted / totalWeight) * 10) / 10;
  }
}

function aiActor() {
  return { type: "ai" as const, id: "ai_engine", name: "Requirements Copilot", model: "claude-sonnet-5" };
}
function pmActor() {
  return { type: "pm" as const, id: "pm_demo", name: "Product Manager" };
}
function stakeholderActor(id: string, name: string) {
  return { type: "stakeholder" as const, id, name };
}

function mkLog(
  action: AuditLogEntry["action"],
  targetType: AuditLogEntry["targetType"],
  targetId: string,
  actor: AuditLogEntry["actor"],
  oldValue: unknown,
  newValue: unknown,
  rationale: string,
  timestamp: string,
): AuditLogEntry {
  return {
    id: `log_${nanoid(8)}`,
    workflowId: WORKFLOW_ID,
    actor,
    action,
    targetType,
    targetId,
    oldValue,
    newValue,
    rationale,
    timestamp,
  };
}

  targetId: string,
  actor: AuditLogEntry["actor"],
  oldValue: unknown,
  newValue: unknown,

    targetType,
    targetId,
    oldValue,
    newValue,
    rationale,
    timestamp,
  };

# BMW Requirements Copilot (v0)

AI-assisted product requirement derivation, prioritization and human-in-the-loop
review for BMW's "AI for Product Decision Making" hackathon challenge.

Read [`docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md`](docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md) first — it has the challenge,
our concept, and how user stories map to what's built. Then read your role doc in
`docs/`.

## Stack

- Next.js 14 (App Router, pinned for Node 18 compatibility — don't bump to 15/16
  mid-hackathon unless everyone upgrades Node to 20+)
- TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 3
- In-memory data store (`src/lib/db.ts`), seeded on boot (`src/lib/seed.ts`) —
  no DB setup required to start working
- Mocked AI layer (`src/lib/ai.ts`) — every function returns realistic
  deterministic output so the app works end-to-end with no API key; swap in
  real Claude calls without touching anything above that layer

## Setup

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000. Requires Node >=18.17 (Node 20+ also fine).

## Project structure

```
src/
  lib/
    types.ts        # shared domain types — the team contract, read this first
    db.ts            # in-memory store + all read/write functions (Role A owns)
    seed.ts          # demo data: one fully-populated "battery" workflow
    ai.ts            # mocked AI functions (Role B replaces internals)
    api-client.ts    # typed fetch wrappers — frontend only talks to the API through here
  app/
    page.tsx                                # landing page (car hotspots)
    workflow/[componentId]/page.tsx         # PM workflow view (Role C)
    stakeholder/[workflowId]/[stakeholderId]/page.tsx  # stakeholder review (Role D)
    api/...                                 # REST routes, thin wrappers around lib/db.ts
  components/        # shared UI: EvidenceBadge, PipelineStrip, AuditLogPanel, RequirementCard, ReviewerRow, CarHotspotViewer
```

## Demo data

The seed pre-populates a **Battery & Charging** workflow for the BMW 5 Series
(Europe market) with 3 requirements, 4 stakeholders, partially-submitted
reviews, and ~17 audit log entries telling a believable story: AI derives a
vague first draft → PM challenges it → AI revises with a concrete target →
stakeholders review → PM is mid-decision. This is what you see immediately on
`npm run dev`, no setup needed. The other 5 components (exterior, interior,
windows, steering, engine) have no workflow yet, to demo the "create new"
flow from the landing page.

## Known tradeoffs (intentional, for a 15-17h build)

- In-memory store, not a real DB. Swap-out point is clearly marked in `db.ts`.
- AI layer is mocked with templated text, not live Claude calls. Swap-out
  point is clearly marked in `ai.ts`, with the exact input/output shape Role
  B needs to preserve.
- Next.js pinned to 14.2.35 (not latest) for Node 18 compatibility across the
  team. `npm audit` will show Next.js platform CVEs fixed only in 15+ — not a
  concern for a localhost demo, but don't deploy this build publicly without
  upgrading first.
- Single demo vehicle/component fully fleshed out rather than breadth across
  all 6 components — depth over breadth for the judged demo.

# Project brief

## The challenge (BMW Group)

> What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers? Build
> an AI-powered application that helps product managers derive, justify, and
> prioritize customer requirements for a successor vehicle. Ground your
> proposals in customer feedback, BMW product and sales data, and relevant web
> research — while keeping the product manager firmly in control of every
> decision.

Scope: BMW 1/5/7 Series (or a combination), Europe/China/US (or a subset),
3-5 years out. For each vehicle we get customer feedback (verbatims),
equipment data, sales volumes, and a customer study; we may enrich with
external sources (competitor info, reviews, market/tech trends).

**What judges want to see** (from the brief, verbatim):
1. A concept + working prototype showing AI supporting identification,
   formulation and prioritization of customer-facing requirements.
2. A representative set of requirements with clear evidence and reasoning.
3. A transparent decision-support experience: PM can review, challenge,
   modify, approve, or reject AI proposals, with evidence/assumptions/
   uncertainties/decisions visible and traceable throughout.

**Explicitly out of scope**: engineering specs, regulatory requirements,
detailed business-case calculations. Focus on customer value.

**Internal framing** (from BMW's own PM keynote, for flavor/credibility in
the demo narrative): the real process goes from ~1 billion findings → ~1,000
requirements → one car. A "requirement" = a customer-relevant attribute of
the car. The real pipeline is: situation analysis → AI structures/clusters/
contextualizes findings → requirements definition (baseline: previous BMW
model, portfolio, sales volume, competition, customer/public feedback,
trends) → specification & quantification (measurable targets, e.g. "range:
600 or 700 mi?") → prioritization → documentation → requirements tracking.
Our workflow pipeline stages mirror this shape.

## Our concept

Three views:

1. **Landing page** — a BMW 5 Series with hotspot dots on components
   (exterior, interior, windows, steering, powertrain, battery). Click a dot:
   open its requirements workflow if one exists, or start a new one.
2. **PM workflow page** (per component) — a GitHub-Actions-style pipeline
   strip (ingest → enrich → extract → derive → score → stakeholder review →
   PM decision → deploy), an AI-generated decision-trail summary, the
   requirement list with explainable scores and adjustable weights, a
   PR-reviewer-style stakeholder panel with an AI overview of where
   reviewers agree/disagree, and a live audit trail sidebar.
3. **Stakeholder review page** — summary of the requirement + evidence
   (charts from real score factors), the AI's running decision-trail
   summary, a free-text expert-opinion field, and approve/not-approve.

**The mechanism that ties it together**: every stage transition, every AI
proposal, every PM decision (approve/reject/postpone/**challenge**), and
every stakeholder review is written to an **append-only audit log**
(`src/lib/types.ts` → `AuditLogEntry`). The AI summaries shown on both the PM
and stakeholder pages are (in the real version) generated *from* that log —
when a PM disagrees and asks for changes, the next AI summary should
narrate what was asked, what was proposed, what the PM pushed back on, and
how the proposal changed. The v0 seed data (`src/lib/seed.ts`) hand-writes
one such story for the battery/charging requirement so the mechanism is
demoable without live AI calls; Role B's job is to make it real.

## User stories → what we're building (prioritized for 15-17h)

We will not build all 9 epics to full depth. Priority order for the time box:

**Must have for the demo (Epics 6, 8, 9, slice of 3/4):**
- US-6.1, 6.2, 6.4 — PM can approve/reject/postpone/challenge with required
  rationale on reject/postpone; evidence shown next to every decision.
  (Built in v0: `RequirementCard`, `PATCH /api/requirements/:id`.)
- US-6.3 — PM challenges a score/rationale, AI re-assesses and states
  whether it changed. (Built in v0 as a mock: `POST /api/requirements/:id/challenge`.)
- US-8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 8.5 — full trace, append-only, actor+timestamp+old/new
  value+rationale on every entry, AI vs human distinguished.
  (Built in v0: `AuditLogEntry`, `logAction()`, `AuditLogPanel`.)
- US-9.1 — defined workflow with stage ownership (ai/pm/stakeholder) shown.
  (Built in v0: `Stage`, `PipelineStrip`.)
- US-3.1, 3.3 — requirements have id, description, linked findings/sources,
  evidence level, assumptions, uncertainties, category, status "Proposed".
  (Built in v0, seeded.)
- US-4.1, 4.2, 4.3 — explainable weighted score, live-adjustable weights,
  evidence level shown next to score. (Built in v0: `scoreFactors`,
  weight sliders in `RequirementCard`.)
- US-7.1, 7.2, 7.3 — missing/thin/contradictory evidence surfaced; weak
  evidence flagged; limitations panel. (Built in v0: `EvidenceBadge`,
  `AISummary` type "limitations".)

**Should have, reach during the build (Epics 1, 2, 5):**
- US-1.1 — real dataset upload/ingestion (v0 only has seeded sources).
- US-2.1 through 2.7 — real signal clustering from uploaded verbatims
  (v0 has a mock `extractSignals()` in `ai.ts`).
- US-5.1 — vehicle/derivative/market selector (v0 only has market at
  workflow-creation time).

**Could have, only if time remains (Epic 1.4, 5.4, 9.2, 9.4, 9.5):**
- Config-driven new data sources, onboarding another model/market without
  code changes, re-running the pipeline on new data with a diff view,
  exporting approved requirements to CSV/Jira.

## Evaluation criteria mapping (from the brief's organizers)

| Criterion | Primary epics | Where in this repo |
|---|---|---|
| Decision and scoring logic | Epic 4, US-7.1 | `scoreFactors`, `EvidenceBadge`, weight sliders |
| Workflow and human decision-making | Epic 6, US-9.1 | `PipelineStrip`, `RequirementCard` actions |
| Traceability and auditability | Epic 8, US-2.6 | `AuditLogPanel`, `logAction()` |
| Solution quality, usability, feasibility | Epics 3, 5, US-4.2 | requirement cards, live weight sliders |
| Innovation, scalability, business impact | US-1.4, 5.4, 9.2 | talk track for the pitch — be honest that this is a v0, point at the swap-out points as the scalability story |

## Non-goals for this hackathon

Do not spend time on: engineering specs, regulatory/homologation detail,
business-case ROI math, auth/accounts, a real database, production
deployment hardening. If in doubt, cut it — a working, honest, traceable
narrow slice beats a broad, flaky one.

# Project brief

## The challenge (BMW Group)

> What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers? Build
> an AI-powered application that helps product managers derive, justify, and
> prioritize customer requirements for a successor vehicle. Ground your
> proposals in customer feedback, BMW product and sales data, and relevant web
> research — while keeping the product manager firmly in control of every
> decision.

Scope: BMW 1/5/7 Series (or a combination), Europe/China/US (or a subset),
3-5 years out. For each vehicle we get customer feedback (verbatims),
equipment data, sales volumes, and a customer study; we may enrich with
external sources (competitor info, reviews, market/tech trends).

**What judges want to see** (from the brief, verbatim):
1. A concept + working prototype showing AI supporting identification,
   formulation and prioritization of customer-facing requirements.
2. A representative set of requirements with clear evidence and reasoning.
3. A transparent decision-support experience: PM can review, challenge,
   modify, approve, or reject AI proposals, with evidence/assumptions/
   uncertainties/decisions visible and traceable throughout.

**Explicitly out of scope**: engineering specs, regulatory requirements,
detailed business-case calculations. Focus on customer value.

**Internal framing** (from BMW's own PM keynote, for flavor/credibility in
the demo narrative): the real process goes from ~1 billion findings → ~1,000
requirements → one car. A "requirement" = a customer-relevant attribute of
the car. The real pipeline is: situation analysis → AI structures/clusters/
contextualizes findings → requirements definition (baseline: previous BMW
model, portfolio, sales volume, competition, customer/public feedback,
trends) → specification & quantification (measurable targets, e.g. "range:
600 or 700 mi?") → prioritization → documentation → requirements tracking.
Our workflow pipeline stages mirror this shape.

Three views:

1. **Landing page** — a BMW 5 Series with hotspot dots on components
   (exterior, interior, windows, steering, powertrain, battery). Click a dot:

   reviewers agree/disagree, and a live audit trail sidebar.

# Role A — Backend & Data Platform

You own `src/lib/types.ts`, `src/lib/db.ts`, `src/lib/seed.ts`, and everything
under `src/app/api/`. You are the team's dependency: Roles C and D build
against `src/lib/api-client.ts`, which already wraps every endpoint that
exists in v0. If you change a response shape, you change `api-client.ts` in
the same commit and shout in the team channel — that file is the contract.

Read `docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md` first for the full picture. This doc is your
task list.

## What already exists (v0, working)

- Full type model in `src/lib/types.ts` — Vehicle, VehicleComponent,
  Workflow/Stage, Requirement/ScoreFactor, Signal, SourceRecord, Stakeholder,
  StakeholderReview, AuditLogEntry, AISummary. Read this file top to bottom
  before changing anything; it's the shared vocabulary.
- In-memory store (`src/lib/db.ts`) with full CRUD + an append-only audit
  log. Every mutation function (`createWorkflow`, `updateStage`,
  `updateRequirementStatus`, `updateWeights`, `submitReview`,
  `addAISummary`) already calls `logAction()` — keep this invariant for
  anything new you add: **no mutation without a log entry**.
- Seed data (`src/lib/seed.ts`) for one fully-populated "battery" workflow.
  This is what makes the demo work without real datasets.
- REST routes for everything in `api-client.ts` — vehicles, components,
  workflows (get/create/by-component), requirements (list/get/patch/
  weights/challenge), signals+sources, audit log, AI summaries,
  stakeholders, reviews.

## Your tasks, roughly in priority order

### 1. Real dataset ingestion (US-1.1, 1.2, 1.3)
Right now sources are hand-seeded. Build:
- `POST /api/workflows/:id/ingest` accepting the four dataset types
  (verbatims, equipment, sales, customer study) as CSV/JSON upload or pasted
  text. Each record becomes a `SourceRecord` with `datasetType`,
  `reliability` (first_party for all internal data), `title`, `excerpt`,
  `retrievedAt`. Malformed rows get flagged in the response, not silently
  dropped (AC in US-1.1) — return `{ imported: n, flagged: [...] }`.
- A minimal web-enrichment step (US-1.2): even a stubbed call to a search
  API or a hardcoded set of competitor data points is fine for the demo —
  the important part is every web `SourceRecord` has `url`, `retrievedAt`,
  and a `reliability` tier (`review_site` / `forum` / `official`), and the
  UI (Role C) can filter by it.
- Wire the `ingest` and `enrich` stages in `Workflow.stages` to flip from
  `pending` → `active` → `complete` as this runs, via `updateStage()`
  (already exists).

### 2. Replace in-memory store with something durable (stretch)
Only if ingestion + everything else is solid with time to spare. SQLite via
`better-sqlite3` or `drizzle` is the fastest path that still ships before a
hackathon deadline — avoid standing up Postgres unless someone already has
it running. Keep every exported function signature in `db.ts` identical;
this should be invisible to Roles B/C/D.

### 3. Multi-market / multi-vehicle support (US-5.1, 5.4)
`Workflow.market` is already a single string set at creation. If time
allows, support comparing requirements across markets for the same
component (US-5.2) — this is a new read endpoint
(`GET /api/components/:id/workflows` returning all market-variant
workflows for a component), not a schema change.

### 4. Pipeline re-run / versioning (US-9.2, 9.3)
Stretch goal: when new data lands, re-run extraction/derivation and show
what changed vs. the last run. Only attempt after everything above is solid
— this is a "could have."

## Guardrails

- Keep `logAction()` calls accurate: `oldValue`/`newValue` should be real
  values, not placeholders — Role B's AI summaries and the audit trail UI
  both depend on these being meaningful, not decorative.
- Don't let the demo break: the seeded "battery" workflow (`wf_battery_demo`)
  is what gets shown to judges if live ingestion isn't finished in time.
  Never modify `seed.ts` in a way that removes that narrative; add new seed
  vehicles/components alongside it instead of replacing it.
- `nanoid` is already a dependency for generating ids — use it instead of
  `Math.random()` or `Date.now()` for anything id-like.

## Files you own

```
src/lib/types.ts
src/lib/db.ts
src/lib/seed.ts
src/app/api/**
```
Coordinate before touching `src/lib/api-client.ts` or `src/lib/ai.ts` —
those are Role B/C/D's primary integration points into your work.

# Role B — AI / Intelligence

You own `src/lib/ai.ts` and the "intelligence" behind the pipeline: turning
raw signals into requirements, scoring them explainably, summarizing
decision history, and re-assessing when the PM pushes back. This is the
feature the judges are most explicitly evaluating ("decision and scoring
logic", "AI supports identification, formulation and prioritization").

Read `docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md` first. Read `src/lib/ai.ts` in full before
writing anything — every function there is a mock with a docstring saying
exactly what real behavior should replace it, and the exact input/output
shape to preserve so Roles A/C/D don't need to change their code when you
swap in real calls.

## How v0 fakes what you're about to make real

The seed data (`src/lib/seed.ts`) hand-writes a believable story for the
"battery" workflow: an AI-drafted requirement that was too vague, a PM
challenge, an AI revision citing specific sources, stakeholder reviews, and
three `AISummary` entries (`decision_trail`, `stakeholder_overview`,
`limitations`) with pre-written narrative text. This is what lets the whole
app demo convincingly before any real AI is wired in. Your job is to make
the mocked functions in `ai.ts` produce *that same quality of narrative*,
generated from real data instead of hand-written.

## Setup

Use the Anthropic SDK with model `claude-sonnet-5`. Get an API key from
whoever on the team has one; store it in `.env.local` as
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (already gitignored). Keep all AI calls server-side
(inside API routes or `lib/ai.ts`, never from a client component) so the
key never ships to the browser.

```bash
npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk
```

## Your tasks, in priority order

### 1. `summarizeDecisionTrail()` (US-9.3, and the "AI summary updates
when PM asks for changes" mechanic from the brief)
Input: a `Requirement` + its related `AuditLogEntry[]` (already wired —
see how `GET /api/workflows/:id/ai-summaries` and the seed seed this).
Real implementation: pass the ordered log entries (especially
`requirement_challenged` and the AI's own prior summaries) to Claude and
ask for a narrative of what was asked, what was proposed, what changed and
why. **This is the single most demo-critical function** — it's the thing
that answers "what happens when a PM disagrees" live, in front of judges.
Test it by calling `POST /api/requirements/:id` with `status: "challenged"`
and a rationale, then regenerating the summary and confirming it reflects
the new log entry.

### 2. `reassessChallenge()` (US-6.3)
Already wired to `POST /api/requirements/:id/challenge`
(`src/app/api/requirements/[id]/challenge/route.ts`). Must return
`{ changed: boolean, explanation: string }` — the AC in US-6.3 explicitly
requires stating whether the challenge changed the result, and why. Prompt
Claude with the requirement's current scoreFactors/evidence and the PM's
free-text argument; have it either adjust `scoreFactors`/`evidenceLevel`
(if so, also call `updateWeights` or extend `db.ts` with a
`updateEvidenceLevel` setter — coordinate with Role A) or explain why
nothing changes.

### 3. `summarizeStakeholderReviews()` (the "PR reviewer" AI overview)
Input: all `StakeholderReview[]` for a requirement. Real implementation:
synthesize where reviewers agree/disagree and *why*, distinguishing a
process objection (like Legal's in the seed data) from a product objection.
This renders directly in the PM workflow page's stakeholder panel.

### 4. `extractSignals()` and `deriveRequirement()` (Epics 2 and 3)
Only once ingestion (Role A) produces real `SourceRecord[]` from uploaded
verbatims. `extractSignals` clusters verbatims into themes with frequency/
sentiment (US-2.1); `deriveRequirement` turns one signal + its sources into
a draft requirement with evidence level, assumptions, uncertainties
(US-3.1). Evidence level should be a real function of source count/
reliability, not vibes — e.g. strong = 3+ sources including first-party,
moderate = 2, weak = 1 or web-only. Keep regulatory/engineering/pricing
findings out of the requirement list (US-3.4) — if a theme is clearly
engineering-only ("battery thermal management"), route it to a
"not a customer requirement" bucket instead of forcing a requirement out of
it; this may need a new field on `Signal` or a new status — coordinate with
Role A before changing `types.ts`.

### 5. Contradiction flagging (US-2.7)
`Signal.contradicts: string[]` already exists in the type but is unused in
seed data beyond being empty arrays. When two signals have opposing
sentiment on a related theme (e.g. "too many screens" vs. "love the
display"), populate this and surface it — Role C can render a warning
badge once this field is populated.

## Guardrails

- Every mocked function's docstring tells you the exact real behavior
  expected and what shape to return — don't change function signatures,
  only bodies, unless you coordinate with whoever's consuming them.
- Use structured output (tool use / JSON mode) for anything whose result
  gets parsed into a typed object (scores, evidence levels) — don't parse
  free text with regex.
- Never let an AI call block the UI with no feedback — if a real call is
  slow, the route should still respond; consider calling these from a
  server action with a loading state Role C/D can show, rather than making
  every page load wait on a live model call. For judge-facing demo
  reliability, consider pre-generating and caching key `AISummary` entries
  for the seeded "battery" workflow rather than regenerating them live
  every page load.

## Files you own

```
src/lib/ai.ts
```
You'll also touch `src/app/api/requirements/[id]/challenge/route.ts` and
possibly add new routes for triggering ingestion→extraction→derivation —
coordinate those additions with Role A.

# Role C — Frontend: PM Experience

You own the landing page and the PM workflow page — the two views a
product manager actually lives in. v0 has a complete, working first draft
of both; your job is to take them from "functionally correct" to
"demo-impressive" and extend them as Role A/B's backend/AI work lands.

Read `docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md` first. Run `npm run dev` and click through
both pages before changing anything — the data flow (landing → create or
open workflow → pipeline → requirements → stakeholder panel → audit log)
already works end to end against the seeded "battery" data.

## What already exists (v0, working)

- `src/app/page.tsx` — landing page. Fetches vehicle + components, renders
  `CarHotspotViewer` with clickable dots, falls back to a plain grid of
  component cards below it. Clicking a dot with no workflow opens a
  "create workflow" modal (market picker → `POST /api/workflows`).
- `src/components/CarHotspotViewer.tsx` — **placeholder** car: an inline SVG
  silhouette with hotspots positioned by `{xPct, yPct}` from
  `VehicleComponent.hotspot`. This is the component to replace with a real
  360 viewer or a proper BMW 5 Series asset.
- `src/app/workflow/[componentId]/page.tsx` — the PM workflow page:
  `PipelineStrip` (stage pipeline), AI decision-trail summary, requirement
  list (`RequirementCard` — score breakdown with live weight sliders,
  approve/reject/postpone/challenge actions), stakeholder review panel
  (`ReviewerRow` list + AI overview) scoped to the selected requirement,
  evidence/sources accordion, limitations panel, and a sticky audit log
  sidebar (`AuditLogPanel`).
- All data access goes through `src/lib/api-client.ts` — don't `fetch()`
  directly in a page/component, add a method there instead if you need a
  new endpoint (coordinate with Role A).

## Your tasks, in priority order

### 1. Real 360 car viewer (the landing page's headline visual)
Replace `CarSilhouette` inside `CarHotspotViewer.tsx`. Options, fastest
first:
- A single high-quality static image (front-3/4 view) with the same
  `{xPct, yPct}` hotspot overlay — zero new dependencies, looks far better
  than the SVG placeholder, lowest risk.
- A real 360 spin (frame sequence + drag-to-rotate, or an embed) if time
  allows — keep the hotspot *positions* driven by data
  (`VehicleComponent.hotspot`), not hardcoded per-frame, or hotspots will
  drift when the car rotates. If you go this route, hotspots probably only
  need to render on the default/front-3-4 frame for v0; don't over-build.
Either way: the "blue dot = has workflow, gray dot = create new" affordance
already works (`CarHotspotViewer` colors by `component.workflowId`) — keep
it.

### 2. Pipeline strip polish (US-9.1)
`PipelineStrip.tsx` already shows stage status (pending/active/complete/
blocked) with hover tooltips (owner, timestamps). As Role A wires real
`ingest`/`enrich` stage transitions, confirm the strip updates live
(poll or re-fetch on an interval, or add a manual refresh button — v0 has
neither, pick whichever is faster to ship). Consider a "re-run pipeline"
button once Role A's US-9.2 lands.

### 3. Sensitivity view (US-4.4, stretch)
`RequirementCard` already lets the PM drag weight sliders and see the score
recompute live (`computeLiveScore`) before saving. For US-4.4, add a view
showing which requirements change rank most as weights shift — this is
naturally a small chart (e.g. a rank-change table or sparkline per
requirement) on the workflow page. Don't build a generic charting library
integration for this — a handful of divs with computed widths (see the bar
"chart" pattern already used in the stakeholder page) is enough.

### 4. Multi-requirement stakeholder panel
Right now the stakeholder review panel on the workflow page scopes to one
`selectedReq` at a time (click a requirement card to select it). If you
have time, consider a workflow-level view that shows review status across
*all* requirements at a glance (e.g. a small reviewer-x-requirement grid),
similar to a PR's "required reviewers" list — only worth it if Role A has
wired multiple requirements with multiple reviews by then.

### 5. Market/vehicle switcher (US-5.1, depends on Role A)
Once Role A exposes multiple workflows per component (different markets),
add a market selector on the workflow page header.

## Guardrails

- Every write action (approve/reject/postpone/challenge/weights) already
  calls `onRequirementChanged` → triggers a full `refresh()` of audit log +
  summaries. Don't bypass this — the audit trail updating live after every
  PM action is core to the demo narrative, not a nice-to-have.
- Reject/postpone require a rationale — this is enforced client-side in
  `RequirementCard` *and* server-side in the API route. Don't remove either
  check.
- Keep the dark theme (`bmw` color tokens in `tailwind.config.ts`) — it's
  already wired through every component.

## Files you own

```
src/app/page.tsx
src/app/workflow/[componentId]/page.tsx
src/components/CarHotspotViewer.tsx
src/components/PipelineStrip.tsx
src/components/RequirementCard.tsx
```
`AuditLogPanel.tsx`, `EvidenceBadge.tsx`, and `ReviewerRow.tsx` are shared
with Role D — coordinate before changing their props.

# Milestones (15-17h build)

v0 already exists on `main` as of kickoff: landing page, PM workflow page,
stakeholder review page, in-memory store, mocked AI layer, one fully
populated demo workflow (BMW 5 Series / Battery & Charging / Europe), all
wired end to end and verified working. Everyone starts from a running app,
not a blank repo — `npm install && npm run dev` should work immediately.

Times are elapsed-from-kickoff, not wall-clock — shift to fit your actual
start time. Each role's detailed task list is in its own doc
(`ROLE_A_BACKEND.md`, `ROLE_B_AI.md`, `ROLE_C_PM_FRONTEND.md`,
`ROLE_D_STAKEHOLDER_TRUST.md`).

## H0 — Kickoff (30 min)
- Everyone: clone, `npm install`, `npm run dev`, click through all three
  views against the seeded data. Confirm you understand the demo narrative
  in `docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md` before writing code.
- Agree on branch strategy: short-lived feature branches off `main`, small
  PRs, merge often (every 1-2h) to avoid a brutal integration at H14. A
  stale branch in a 16h hackathon is a dead branch.
- Role A: get an Anthropic API key into the team's hands for Role B.
- Everyone: confirm Node version (`node -v`) — 18.17+ required, 20+ fine.

## H0:30 - H4 — Parallel build, independent tracks
- **Role A**: dataset ingestion endpoint (US-1.1) — CSV/paste upload for the
  four dataset types, malformed-row flagging, `SourceRecord` creation.
  Start on a second seeded component (e.g. "interior") in parallel so
  there's a second demo-able story by H8.
- **Role B**: wire the Anthropic SDK, get `summarizeDecisionTrail()`
  producing real output against the seeded battery audit log. This is the
  highest-leverage function in the app — prioritize it over everything
  else in your doc.
- **Role C**: real car visual for the landing page (static image + hotspot
  overlay, minimum; 360 viewer if time allows). This is the first thing
  judges see — don't let it stay a wireframe SVG past H4.
- **Role D**: standalone audit trail view with filtering (US-8.1, 8.4).

**Checkpoint H4**: everyone demos their piece to the group, 2 min each.
Merge anything stable into `main`.

## H4 - H8 — Integration + depth
- **Role A**: wire real `ingest`/`enrich` stage transitions to the pipeline
  strip so Role C's UI shows real progress, not just seeded "complete"
  states. Start on multi-market support if ingestion is solid.
- **Role B**: `reassessChallenge()` and `summarizeStakeholderReviews()` real
  implementations. Test the full "PM challenges → AI re-assesses → states
  whether it changed" loop live against the UI.
- **Role C**: pipeline strip polish, live-refresh on stage changes, start
  the sensitivity view (US-4.4) if the weight-slider mechanic needs it to
  feel complete.
- **Role D**: audit log CSV export, low-confidence queue (US-7.2).

**Checkpoint H8 (roughly halfway)**: full run-through as a group, PM
persona end to end: land → open/create a workflow → review requirements →
challenge one → see stakeholder reviews come in → approve. Fix anything
that breaks this path before adding more features — this path *is* the
demo.

## H8 - H12 — Breadth + second component
- Get a second component (beyond battery) demo-ready end to end, ideally
  one where the PM *rejects* a requirement (shows the full decision
  spectrum, not just approve). Role A seeds/ingests it, Role B's AI
  functions run against it for real, Roles C/D confirm the UI holds up
  with different data shapes (e.g. a requirement with zero stakeholder
  reviews yet, or all-reject).
- Epic 2 signal extraction (`extractSignals`, Role B) from real verbatims,
  if ingestion (Role A) is ready.
- Stretch items from each role's doc, time permitting, in the priority
  order listed there — don't start a role's "stretch" section if their
  "must have" isn't demo-stable yet.

## H12 - H14 — Feature freeze, bug bash
- **No new features after H12** unless something is badly broken. Switch
  entirely to: click through every view on a clean `npm install && npm run
  dev`, fix what's broken, tighten copy, fix loading/empty states.
- Confirm `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx next lint` are both clean.
- Confirm the demo narrative survives a hard refresh at every step (no
  state that only exists because of a specific click order).

## H14 - H16 — Demo prep
- Write the 3-minute demo script: landing page (show the concept) → open
  battery workflow (show pipeline + AI summary) → challenge a requirement
  live (show the AI re-assessment loop — this is your best "wow" moment) →
  switch to stakeholder view, submit a review (show it land back in the PM
  view's audit trail) → show the audit log / traceability view (prove the
  "transparent decision-support" claim from the brief).
- Record a fallback screen capture of the full demo in case live demo
  breaks — `npm run build && npm run start` once to confirm production
  build works, not just dev mode.
- Prepare the pitch framing around the evaluation criteria table in
  `docs/PROJECT_BRIEF.md` — name-check "decision and scoring logic",
  "traceability and auditability", etc. explicitly, since that's literally
  how this gets scored.

## H16 - H17 — Buffer
Things go wrong. This hour exists so that when they do, you're not cutting
into demo prep.
